text: , Tioclomarol, p.1413 p.1284 Warfarin, p.1425 Antiplatelet drugs Platelet aggregation is important in haemostasis (p.1045) and is also involved in thrombus formation, particularly in the arterial circulation. Antiplatelet drugs reduce platelet aggregation and are used to prevent further thromboem- bolic events in patients who have suffered myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attacks, or unstable angina, and for primary prevention of a throm- boembolic event in patients at risk. Some are also used for the prevention of reocclusion or restenosis following angi- oplasty and bypass procedures. Antiplatelet drugs act through a wide range of mecha- nisms. Aspirin (p.20) is the most widely used and studied; it acts by irreversibly inhibiting platelet cyclo-oxygenase and thus preventing synthesis of thromboxane A2. Revers- ible cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors such as indobufen are also available, and thromboxane synthase inhibitors and thromboxane receptor antagonists have also been used. Drugs that interfere with adenosine metabolism have an antiplatelet effect and those used include some prostaglan- dins, which act by increasing platelet cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels; the thienopyridines clopidogrel and ticlopidine, which interfere with adenosine diphos- phate mediated platelet activation; and the adenosine reuptake inhibitor dipyridamole. Thrombin inhibitors such as heparin and the hirudins have antiplatelet and anticoagulant effects. Glycoprotein IIb/II- Ia-receptor antagonists, such as abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban, interfere with the final step in platelet aggre- gation and are used in unstable angina and as adjuncts in reperfusion and revascularisation procedures. References.
